content: West Nile Virus (WNV) was first isolated in 1937 from a hospitalized patient in the West Nile district of Northern Uganda who presented with an isolated fever. Between 1950 and 1960, small villages in the Mediterranean basin, particularly in Israel and Egypt, experienced repeated outbreaks. These outbreaks provided researchers with opportunities to study the molecular and clinical characteristics of the disease, as well as its mode of transmission and natural history. Several WNV outbreaks were documented in the latter half of the 20th century across Europe, the Middle East, the Far East, and Africa. However, it was not until 1999 that the first outbreak in the United States was recorded, marking WNV as a global infection. The most severe outbreak occurred in 2002 in the United States, with the highest number of cases of meningoencephalitis ever recorded from a single WNV outbreak. In the same year, the first documented cases of person-to-person transmission were reported, involving blood transfusions and tissue transplantation. The initial discovery of WNV occurred in 1937 when it was isolated from a patient in Uganda. Early reports described the virus as having physical and pathological characteristics similar to those of St. Louis encephalitis virus and Japanese encephalitis virus. Early studies also noted the virus's neurotropism, as it frequently involved the central nervous system (CNS) in infected patients. However, it was during the 1950-1960 outbreaks in the Mediterranean basin that the clinical and pathological features of WNV were more thoroughly characterized. The first epidemic of WNV was documented in 1951 in Israel, where Bernkopf and colleagues isolated the virus from 123 cases. Subsequent studies during outbreaks in Cairo, Egypt, between 1951 and 1954 further elucidated the viral transmission patterns and pathogenesis. In 1957, during another outbreak in Israel, the first reports of neurological sequelae following WNV infection were documented. Later outbreaks in regions such as Europe, India, and South Africa were described in the 1970s and 1980s. A significant outbreak in Romania in 1996 triggered a series of outbreaks in the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe. Unlike earlier reports that primarily involved children, these outbreaks revealed a predominance of adult cases and an increased rate of CNS complications. In 1999, the first outbreak in the United States was reported in Queens, New York City, involving eight cases, most of which presented with neurological symptoms. This outbreak marked the global spread of WNV and eventually infected 62 individuals, many of whom required hospitalization due to severe symptoms. Initially thought to be caused by an endemic arbovirus, WNV was identified as the causative agent after a concurrent outbreak among infected birds in the same region and timeframe. By 2002, the most clinically severe WNV outbreak occurred in North America, with the largest number of meningoencephalitis cases ever recorded. That same year, human-to-human transmission via blood transfusion and tissue transplantation was identified for the first time. The first commercial diagnostic test for WNV, based on MAC-ELISA, was developed and later commercialized for field use. The WNV-DNA vaccine is currently the only USDA-approved vaccine for the virus. The 1999 outbreak in New York prompted the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to establish a Zoo Surveillance Program at Cornell University’s School of Veterinary Medicine. During the outbreak, the CDC also initiated testing of infected bird species to help identify the virus. Delays in diagnosis were considered a significant factor contributing to the outbreak's adverse outcomes. Following the 1999 outbreak, WNV was designated a nationally reportable disease in the United States. Annual meetings were held to disseminate public health information about WNV, and guidelines for surveillance, prevention, and control were developed and regularly updated. In 2000, the CDC launched ArboNET, a real-time disease reporting network, to monitor WNV infections in humans and animals. Initially funded with $7 million, the program’s budget increased to over $20 million within a few years. Grants were used to train arbovirologists, fund research programs, and support laboratory diagnostics and surveillance initiatives.
